explanation: Virtual memory is a memory-management technique that provides each process with its own private address space, independent of physical memory. This allows processes to run concurrently without interfering with each other and enables efficient use of physical memory.  Address translation, implemented via mechanisms like paging and segmentation, maps virtual addresses used by processes to physical addresses in RAM.
syntax: The general approach involves a multi-level page table structure. A virtual address is broken down into a virtual page number (VPN) and a page offset. The VPN is used to index into page tables to locate the corresponding physical frame number (PFN), which, combined with the page offset, forms the physical address.
code_example:
; Example illustrating a simplified address translation (conceptual)
; Assume a two-level page table with 10-bit VPN and 10-bit page offset
; Assume page table entries are 4 bytes (32 bits)
mov eax, [virtual_address]; Load virtual address into eax
mov ebx, eax; Copy virtual address
shr ebx, 10; Shift right by 10 bits to extract VPN
mov ecx, page_table_base; Load base address of level 1 page table
mov edx, [ecx + ebx * 4]; Load entry from level 1 page table
mov ecx, edx; ecx now holds base address of level 2 page table
mov ebx, eax; Restore original virtual address
and ebx, 0x3FF; Mask out page offset (10 least significant bits)
add edx, ebx; Add page offset to obtain physical address in edx
; Now edx holds the physical address
example_explanation: The code snippet demonstrates a simplified two-level page table translation.  It shows how the virtual address is broken into VPN and page offset. The VPN is used to index into the page table(s) to find the corresponding PFN. This PFN is combined with the page offset to get the physical address. This illustrates the fundamental mechanism of address translation, a core component of virtual memory management.  Note that this is a high-level conceptual example and omits many details of a real-world implementation, such as handling page faults and TLBs.
